knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 5.1.3
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly describes the inputs and output object for a simple posterior calculation?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Posterior is the updated distribution. Point estimators under loss and intervals are subsequent summaries, not automatic byproducts of writing posterior.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Prior plus likelihood give posterior distribution. Loss-based point estimate is a further step.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Treating posterior as automatically delivering loss-based point estimator.

choices.label: Prior and likelihood together yield a posterior distribution for the parameter. A loss-based point estimator is a further step summarising that posterior under a chosen loss function.
Having the posterior distribution automatically finishes choosing the Bayesian point estimator under squared-error loss; no further step exists.
Simple posterior means the prior alone; likelihood enters only in frequentist confidence intervals.
The output object is always a credible interval; a full posterior distribution is unnecessary once data are observed.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 5.1.3
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Binomial n=10 with x=3 successes and Beta(2,2) prior. Which statement is correct?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Conjugate update adds successes to first shape and failures to second: Beta(5,9). Posterior mean under squared-error loss is a separate summary step.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Posterior Beta(5,9). Refuse posterior as automatic loss estimator.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Stopping at prior, sample proportion, or treating posterior as automatic point estimator.

choices.label: Posterior Beta(2+3, 2+7) = Beta(5,9). The posterior is the full distribution; a loss-based point estimator (for example posterior mean under squared-error loss) is a further step.
Posterior Beta(2,2) because the prior dominates with n=10 small; successes add nothing to the parameters.
Posterior mean 3/10 = 0.3 is the posterior distribution; Beta(5,9) is optional notation.
Having Beta(5,9) finishes choosing the Bayesian point estimator under squared-error loss without calculation.

worked_example.title: Posterior for Exponential rate with Gamma prior
worked_example.problem_statement: Claim waiting times (months) are Exponential with rate λ. The prior is Gamma(α, β) with shape-rate parameterisation π(λ) ∝ λ^{α−1} e^{−βλ}, here α = 4, β = 6. A sample of n = 5 independent waiting times has sum Σxᵢ = 8. Obtain the posterior distribution and its mean.

given.note: sample size and total waiting time

worked_example.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Update shape by +n and rate by +Σxᵢ, then mean = shape/rate.

steps.label: Likelihood structure
steps.attempt_cue: Recall L(λ) ∝ λ^n exp(−λ Σxᵢ) for Exponential waiting times.
steps.explanation: The posterior combines prior and likelihood. For Exponential rate with a Gamma prior, the update stays Gamma.

steps.label: Posterior mean
steps.explanation: A point estimate from the posterior (e.g. under squared error) is a separate loss step; here report the posterior mean.

worked_example.final_answer: Posterior is Gamma(9, 14) with mean 9/14 ≈ 0.6429 per month.
worked_example.common_pitfall: Updating only the shape (Gamma(9, 6)) or using the MLE λ̂ = n/Σxᵢ = 5/8 = 0.625 as if it were already the full posterior object.
